title: Increased reproductive success of women after prenatal undernutrition.
ehr_evidence: The medical birth records provided information about the mother, the course of the pregnancy and the size of the baby and the placenta at birth. Socio-economic status (SES) of the mothers was based on the occupation of the head of the family at the time of delivery and classified as either manual or non-manual, using the information provided by the birth records. Trained nurses carried out all interviews to collect reproductive and demographic data.
summary: Investigation of whether prenatal exposure to the Dutch famine of 1944–1945 affected reproductive success (number of children, twinning, age at first delivery, childlessness) in a historical birth cohort traced at age 58.
key_findings: F1 women exposed in utero had more children (mean 2.0 vs 1.7, P=0.002).
Exposed women were younger at first delivery (23.2 vs 23.7 years, P=0.05).
Exposed women had higher twinning rates (OR 2.7 [95% CI 1.1 to 7.0]).
Exposed women were less likely to be childless (OR 0.80 [95% CI 0.66–0.98]).
Adjusted HR for age at first delivery was 0.8 [95% CI 0.6–1.0].
In F1 men, prenatal famine exposure was not associated with any alterations in reproductive success.
captured_features: duration of delay to first pregnancy
study_design: historical birth cohort study with follow-up interviews
data_source_type: historical birth registry and follow-up surveys
population: 2414 live-born singletons born in Amsterdam, Netherlands (1943-1947); 855 participants traced at age 58 (473 women, 382 men)
limitations: 55% participation rate may introduce selection bias
reliance on self-reported reproductive history via interviews
unable to fully rule out genetic confounding for fertility traits
